## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Isigili Sutta* (MN 116; PTS MN iii 68) is set at Mount Isigili near Rājagaha [SuttaCentral; Ray 1994; Walker 2018]. Reflecting on the impermanence of geographical features, the Buddha relates how five hundred *paccekabuddhas* (solitary or silent buddhas) formerly dwelled on Mount Isigili [SuttaCentral; Jantrasrisalai 2008; Walker 2018]. In the discourse, these figures are presented as *ṛṣis* (*isi*) and contrasted with ordinary mortals (*manussa*) [Ray 1994]. Structurally, the text provides an enumeration of the names of these past sages in prose followed by an expanded metric list in verse, concluding with an exhortation to pay homage to them [Norman 1983; Walker 2018]. Modern philologists note that the third *paṇṇāsa* of the *Majjhimanikāya*, within which the sutta is preserved, includes material of relatively late composition, and Norman suggests that the systematized lists of *paccekabuddhas* in MN 116 reflect later developments or borrowings in early Buddhist literature [Norman 1983].

A direct parallel to the sutta is found in the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 38.7) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2010]. Algorithmic alignment by DharmaNexus confirms this correspondence with the *Ekottarika-āgama* (ZH_T02_0125_032) and shows further textual links to the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (ZH_T02_0100_016) and Tibetan works such as the *Udānavargavivaraṇa* (D4100) [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus records 241 reused segments across 29 canonical and post-canonical works, sharing substantial stock formulas with the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8), and *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), as well as exegesis in the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

Beyond canonical study, the *Isigili Sutta* occupies an important role in protective (*paritta*) ritual culture [Global Recovery 2010; Walker 2018]. In Sri Lanka, it is included in the Book of Protection (*Pirith Potha*) as one of five special *parittas* recited to heal and dispel illness [Global Recovery 2010]. In Southeast Asian manuscript traditions, such as Cambodian chanted accordion books (*leporellos*), the text is preserved for liturgical recitation and organized into three melodic recitation units (*pad*), dividing the opening prose and the subsequent poetic verses [Walker 2018].
